subtopics.title: Fusion and pressure welding
subtopics.theory_md:
**Welding** permanently joins metals by heat, with or without pressure and filler, so they coalesce.
- **Fusion (non-pressure)**: edges melted, filler usually added, no pressure. Gas (oxy-acetylene), arc (SMAW, carbon, TIG, MIG, submerged, plasma), thermit, electron beam, laser.
- **Pressure (plastic)**: heated to a plastic state (or not at all) and pressed. Forge (heated in a forge to about 1200 to 1300 $^\circ$C and hammered), resistance (spot, seam, projection, butt, flash), friction, ultrasonic, explosive, diffusion.

Resistance heat: $H = I^2Rt$. Arc about 3500 $^\circ$C, oxy-acetylene flame about 3200 $^\circ$C.
subtopics.basics_md: Two ways to join metal: melt the edges so they flow together (fusion), or soften them and squeeze them together (pressure).
key_points: Welding = joining by heat, with or without pressure and filler
Fusion: gas, arc, thermit, electron beam, laser (no pressure)
Pressure: forge, resistance, friction, ultrasonic, explosive
Resistance welding is a pressure process, heat $I^2Rt$
Forge welding: forge heat, plastic state, hammering, no filler

subtopics.title: Welding, brazing and soldering
subtopics.theory_md:
In **welding** the base metal melts (fusion) and the joint is about as strong as the parent metal, at 1500 $^\circ$C and above.

In **brazing** a filler (brass, Cu-Zn, silver alloys) melting **above 450 $^\circ$C** but below the base metal fills the joint by capillary action; the base metal does **not** melt. Medium strength: tools, pipes.

In **soldering** the filler (Pb-Sn) melts **below 450 $^\circ$C**; base metal not melted. Lowest strength: electronics, tin work. Some books use 427 $^\circ$C (800 $^\circ$F).
subtopics.basics_md: Welding melts the parts themselves. Brazing and soldering melt only a glue-like filler between solid parts; the dividing line between them is 450 $^\circ$C.
key_points: Welding: base metal melts, strongest joint
Brazing: filler above 450 $^\circ$C, base metal not melted
Soldering: filler below 450 $^\circ$C, base metal not melted
Filler flows by capillary action in brazing and soldering
Strength order: welding > brazing > soldering

subtopics.title: Gas welding and its flames
subtopics.theory_md:
**Gas welding**: a flame of acetylene burning in oxygen melts the edges; a filler rod and flux are added; no pressure. Oxy-acetylene neutral flame about 3200 $^\circ$C.

**Equipment**: oxygen (black) and acetylene (maroon) cylinders, regulators with gauges, hoses (oxygen green, acetylene red), torch with mixing chamber and nozzle, filler rod, flux, goggles, gloves, spark lighter, flash-back arrestor.

| Flame | O$_2$ : C$_2$H$_2$ | Look | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neutral | about 1 : 1 | bright inner cone, blue envelope | mild steel, cast iron, copper |
| Oxidising | excess O$_2$ (about 1.5 : 1) | short, pointed, hissing | brass, bronze |
| Carburising (reducing) | excess C$_2$H$_2$ | white feather round cone | aluminium, hard facing, high-carbon steel |
subtopics.basics_md: A gas torch is a controlled flame. The mix of oxygen and fuel gas decides how hot it is and whether it adds or removes oxygen at the metal.

Neutral flame O$_2$:C$_2$H$_2$ about 1:1, hottest, steel and copper

questions.q: What is gas welding? How are neutral, oxidising and reducing flames obtained, and where is each used?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Gas welding**: fusion process using a flame of acetylene in oxygen (about 3200 $^\circ$C) with filler rod and flux; no pressure.

**Obtaining the flames** (by the torch valves)
1. **Neutral**: light acetylene (smoky yellow flame), add oxygen until the feather vanishes and a sharp inner cone appears; O$_2$:C$_2$H$_2$ about 1:1. Use: mild steel, cast iron, copper.

subtopics.title: Welded joints and fillet weld
subtopics.theory_md:
**Joints** (how the parts meet): **butt** (edge to edge in one plane; square, V, U, double-V), **lap** (overlapped, fillet welded), **T** (one plate perpendicular to the other), **corner** (right angle at a corner), **edge** (parallel plates, edges welded).

**Weld types** (the bead itself): fillet, groove (butt), plug, spot.

Fillet weld of leg $s$: the **throat** is $t = s\cos45^\circ = 0.707\,s$ and the strength of one weld of length $l$ is $P = 0.707\,s\,l\,\tau$, with permissible shear stress $\tau$. The throat, not the leg, carries the load.
subtopics.basics_md: A joint is how two plates sit against each other. A weld is the metal you lay in it. A fillet weld is a triangle; its weakest cut is the short line from corner to face, the throat.
key_points: Five joints: butt, lap, T, corner, edge
Joint type is different from weld type (fillet, groove)
Lap and T joints use fillet welds, butt uses groove welds
Throat $t = 0.707\,s$ of the leg
Fillet strength $P = 0.707\,s\,l\,\tau$

subtopics.title: Weldability
subtopics.theory_md:
**Weldability** is the ease with which a metal can be welded into a sound joint of the required properties, free of cracks, porosity and distortion, by ordinary procedures.

It **depends on**: chemical composition (carbon equivalent; carbon, sulphur, phosphorus lower it), thermal conductivity and expansion, melting point, surface oxide films (Al, stainless steel), thickness, process and filler or flux, preheat and joint design, and welder skill.

Low-carbon steel: good. High-carbon steel and cast iron: poor, they harden and crack, so preheat. The **heat-affected zone (HAZ)** is the base metal that is heated but does not melt.
subtopics.basics_md: A metal with good weldability forgives mistakes. Metals that crack when they cool quickly, or that grow a stubborn oxide skin, do not.
key_points: Weldability = ease of making a sound joint
Depends on composition, conductivity, expansion, oxide films, process, preheat
Low-carbon steel good; high-carbon steel and cast iron poor
HAZ is heated but not melted

|---|---|---|

subtopics.title: Principle of arc welding
subtopics.theory_md:
An **electric arc** is struck between the electrode and the job. Touch the electrode to the work and withdraw it 2 to 4 mm: current keeps flowing through the ionised gas as a bright arc at about **3500 to 6000 $^\circ$C**. The heat melts the edges of the base metal and the electrode tip; they fuse in a pool and solidify as the weld. No pressure is used (fusion welding).

Arc voltage 20 to 40 V, current 50 to 600 A, supplied by a transformer (AC) or rectifier or generator (DC). Arc power $P = VI$. Heat input per length $H = \dfrac{\eta VI}{v}$ with travel speed $v$.
subtopics.basics_md: A spark that is made to stay alive. A low voltage, very high current keeps a gap of hot ionised gas glowing, and that heat does the melting.
key_points: Arc between electrode and job gives the heat

Melts base metal and electrode, pool solidifies to weld
Fusion process, no pressure

subtopics.title: Shielded metal arc welding (SMAW)
subtopics.theory_md:
**SMAW** (stick or metal arc welding): a flux-coated consumable electrode in a holder; supply connected between electrode and work. Once the arc is struck (20 to 40 V, 50 to 400 A) the core wire and base metal melt. The coating gives a **gas shield** and a **slag** blanket. Keep arc length about the core diameter and the electrode at 70 to 80$^\circ$ to the plate; chip the slag when cooled.

**Preparing rusted mild steel**: wire brush, grind or blast off rust and scale; degrease with solvent; clean bright 25 mm each side; bevel thick plate; use dry low-hydrogen electrodes.
subtopics.basics_md: A stick of filler wrapped in a protective coating. As it burns, the coating makes its own gas and crust so the molten pool never meets air.
key_points: Coated consumable electrode, holder, source and earth return
Arc melts core wire and base metal
Coating gives gas shield and slag

subtopics.title: Polarity and flux
subtopics.theory_md:
**Polarity** is how the electrode is connected to the terminals of a **DC** source. The anode (positive) gets more heat, about two thirds.
- **Straight polarity (DCEN/DCSP)**: electrode negative, work positive. More heat at the work: **deep penetration**, thick plates, slower electrode melting.
- **Reverse polarity (DCEP/DCRP)**: electrode positive, work negative. More heat at the electrode: **shallow penetration**, faster melting, thin sheets, non-ferrous metals, oxide cleaning.
- **AC**: no polarity, heat shared equally.

**Flux** in arc welding (the coating): gas shield, slag, arc stabiliser, deoxidiser. In gas welding, borax-type flux dissolves oxides on cast iron, brass, aluminium and stainless steel.
subtopics.basics_md: Where electrons crash in, heat is released. Put the work on the positive side and the plate gets hotter and melts deeper; swap them and the electrode gets hotter instead.
key_points: Polarity applies to DC only; AC has none
Straight: electrode negative, work positive, deep penetration
Reverse: electrode positive, work negative, shallow, thin sheets and non-ferrous
About 2/3 of heat at the positive terminal
Flux: gas, slag, arc stability, deoxidation; gas welding flux removes oxides

subtopics.title: What arc blow is and why it happens
subtopics.theory_md:
**Arc blow** is the **deflection of the arc** from its intended path by **magnetic forces**.

DC current in the electrode, arc and work sets up magnetic fields. The arc is a flexible current-carrying column, so when the field is **unbalanced** it is pushed sideways. This happens near the ends of plates, in corners, at gaps, near a large ferromagnetic mass, and with an off-centre earth clamp.

**Effects**: spatter, poor fusion and penetration, irregular bead, porosity. It occurs in **DC**; AC rarely suffers because the field keeps reversing. Wind is not arc blow.
subtopics.basics_md: Current makes a magnetic field. A bending current path or a lump of iron near the arc makes the field lopsided, and the arc gets shoved sideways like a flame in a draught.
key_points: Arc blow = arc deflected by magnetic fields
Cause: unbalanced field of DC current in work and arc
Occurs at plate ends, corners, gaps, heavy ferrous masses, wrong earth position
Effects: spatter, poor penetration, irregular bead
Mainly a DC problem; wind is not the cause

subtopics.title: Remedies for arc blow
subtopics.theory_md:
Remedies work by **restoring a balanced magnetic field**, or by removing the field:
1. Use **AC** (field keeps reversing).
2. **Shorten the arc** (less arm for the force to act on).
3. **Change the earth clamp position**, usually to the far end of the joint, or use two earths.
4. Reduce the **current**; use **back-step** welding.
5. Place **run-off tabs** or tack the ends; weld towards the heavy mass or the direction of the blow.
6. **Demagnetise** the job; keep ferrous masses away.

An answer that lists remedies without the cause loses marks.
subtopics.basics_md: If a lopsided field is the problem, balance it (move the earth), shorten the part the field can push (short arc), or switch to a current whose field keeps flipping (AC).
key_points: Use AC instead of DC
Short arc and reduced current
Move earth clamp or use two earths
Back-step, run-off tabs, tack welds
Demagnetise the job

subtopics.title: The SMAW setup and power source
subtopics.theory_md:
**Equipment**: power source, welding cables (electrode lead and earth lead), electrode holder, earth (work) clamp, electrodes, welding table, protective gear, chipping hammer, wire brush, tongs.

subtopics.title: Duty cycle and ratings
subtopics.theory_md:
**Duty cycle** is the percentage of a 10-minute period for which a source can deliver its rated current without overheating: $D = \dfrac{\text{arc-on time}}{10\ \text{min}} \times 100$. A 60% duty cycle means 6 min welding, 4 min rest.

At another current $I_2$: $D_2 = D_1\left(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}\right)^2$ (heating is proportional to $I^2$).

Current for continuous (100%) use: $I_{100} = I_r\sqrt{D_r}$ with $D_r$ as a fraction.

The transformer **steps voltage down**, never up. OCV (about 50 to 100 V) is higher than the arc voltage.
subtopics.basics_md: A machine heats up while it welds and cools while it rests. A duty cycle says how big a fraction of each ten minutes it may work flat out.
key_points: Duty cycle = arc-on time / 10 min $\times$ 100
60% duty = 6 min on, 4 min off
Period is 10 min, not 1 hour

questions.q: The same 300 A, 60% set is used at 350 A. Find the permissible duty cycle, and the arc-on time in each 10 minutes.
questions.model_answer_md:
$D_2 = D_1\left(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}\right)^2 = 0.6 \times \left(\dfrac{300}{350}\right)^2 = 0.6 \times 0.7347 = 0.441$

Duty cycle about **44%**, so arc-on time = $0.441 \times 10 = 4.4$ min in each 10 min.

subtopics.title: Hand tools, protective gear and safety
subtopics.theory_md:
**Chipping hammer**: chisel head and pointed tail; **chips slag** from the cooled bead between passes so no slag is trapped. **Wire brush** cleans after chipping. **Tongs** hold hot work. **Helmet or hand shield with filter glass** protects eyes and face from arc rays and spatter.

**Safety**: leather gloves, apron and safety shoes; dry clothes and hands; ventilation and fume extraction; no flammable material near; check cables, insulation and earthing; switch off before changing the electrode; screens for others; let hot metal cool and mark it; fire extinguisher ready. For gas welding add flash-back arrestors, upright secured oil-free cylinders and leak checks.

subtopics.title: Choosing between AC and DC
subtopics.theory_md:
**Why AC is harder**: at 50 Hz the current passes through zero **100 times per second**, and the arc tries to go out each time. Ionising agents (sodium, potassium compounds) in the coating keep the gap conductive, so electrodes for AC are specially coated; bare ones do not work.

**Choose DC** for thin sheets, non-ferrous metals and stainless steel (reverse polarity), deep penetration (straight polarity), and easy arc striking with small electrodes.

**Choose AC** for thick steel plate in ordinary workshops: cheap, low maintenance, **no arc blow**, no polarity to set.
subtopics.basics_md: AC is a current that swings to zero twice every cycle. The coating keeps the hot gas ready to conduct again straight away.
key_points: 50 Hz AC gives 100 current zeros per second
Coating with ionising agents re-ignites the arc
DC for thin sheet, non-ferrous, stable arc
AC for cheap general work, no arc blow

questions.q: On AC, electrodes need ionising agents in the coating because

questions.why: The ions keep the gap conducting while the current passes through zero.

options: DC straight polarity with a very high current
questions.why: Reverse polarity gives shallow penetration and oxide cleaning.

questions.q: How many times per second does the arc tend to extinguish on 50 Hz AC? Why?
questions.model_answer_md: In each cycle the current is zero twice (at the end of each half cycle). So $2 \times 50 = 100$ times per second. The arc is re-ignited by the OCV and by ionising agents in the electrode coating.
points: Two zeros per cycle
100 per second
Re-ignition by OCV and coating

**AC**: ordinary thick steel work where cost matters, and jobs where arc blow is a problem.

subtopics.title: Purpose and types of electrodes
subtopics.theory_md:
**Purpose**: an electrode (1) carries current and maintains the arc, (2) in consumable types supplies **filler metal**, (3) its coating shields the pool, stabilises the arc and forms slag.

- **Non-consumable**: carbon or graphite (carbon arc, brazing), **tungsten** (TIG, with inert gas); filler added separately.
- **Consumable**: **bare** (poor quality, rare), **flux-coated** (most common): light-coated (stabilises arc) and heavy-coated (structural quality).

By coating: **cellulose** (E6010, deep penetration, pipelines), **rutile** (E6013, easy, general work and sheet), **basic or low-hydrogen** (E7018, high strength, pressure vessels), iron-powder (high deposition).
subtopics.basics_md: Some electrodes only carry the current and stay whole (tungsten, carbon). Others carry current and also melt into the joint as filler, usually wearing a coating.

subtopics.title: Electrode coating: composition and functions
subtopics.theory_md:
**Composition**: arc stabilisers (sodium or potassium silicates, titanium dioxide), gas formers (cellulose, starch, limestone giving CO$_2$), slag formers (rutile, silica, lime, fluorspar), deoxidisers (ferro-manganese, ferro-silicon), alloying elements (Cr, Ni, Mo), iron powder, and a **binder** (sodium silicate).

**Functions**
1. Stabilises the arc.
2. Gas shield against O$_2$ and N$_2$.
3. Slag covers, slows cooling, shapes the bead.
4. Deoxidises and cleans the pool.
5. Adds alloying elements and filler (iron powder).
6. Supports metal in vertical and overhead work.
7. Insulates the core wire and focuses the arc.
subtopics.basics_md: The coating is the electrode's coat of armour: when it burns it releases gas and melts to a crust that keeps air off the weld.

subtopics.title: Electrode coding and selection
subtopics.theory_md:
**AWS code**, e.g. **E6013**: E = electrode; first two digits = tensile strength in ksi (60 ksi = 60 $\times$ 6.895 = **413.7 MPa**); third digit = **position** (1 = all positions); last digit = coating and current type (3 = rutile, AC or DC). **E7018**: 70 ksi = 482.65 MPa, low hydrogen, pressure vessels. **E6010**: cellulose, DC reverse, deep penetration.

Electrode size means the **core wire diameter**. Rule of thumb: current $I \approx (35 \text{ to } 40)\,d$ amperes for $d$ in mm.

**Select by**: base metal, thickness, position, current type (AC or DC), joint, required strength.
subtopics.basics_md: The letters and digits are a label: strength first, then where you may use it, then what coating and current it likes.
key_points: E = electrode, first two digits strength in ksi
